facts.claim: "I Don't Recall" is the third track on Lavender Diamond's album Incorruptible Heart, which came out in 2012 on Paracadute.
Songwriting credits for the track list Rebecca Stark, Damian Kulash Jr., Steve Gregoropoulos, Ronald Rege Jr. and Jeff Rosenberg.
Incorruptible Heart was produced by Damian Kulash of OK Go, who is a childhood friend of Becky Stark. Both attended Brown University.
Kulash also played on the album. He suggested that Stark gather her many songs and treat them as one batch.
The album was mixed by Dave Fridmann of the Flaming Lips.
The music video for "I Don't Recall" was directed by Jena Malone and released in April 2013.

Lavender Diamond said the video was inspired by Andrew Wyeth's painting "Christina's World". They said it takes a lighthearted, humorous tone toward the therapeutic side of dealing with a broken heart.
Incorruptible Heart is Lavender Diamond's second full-length album and followed Imagine Our Love (2007), which was released on Matador.
Stark said she asked Kulash for advice because she had written a huge number of songs. He offered to produce the record, and Paracadute was then able to release it.
The name Lavender Diamond comes from a character Stark played in a punk puppet operetta by Xander Marro. Stark met bandmate Ron Rege in Providence, Rhode Island.

research.lineage: Lavender Diamond is a Los Angeles-based indie-pop and folk band led by Becky Stark, and Incorruptible Heart mixes 1950s pop, 1970s disco and electronic textures.

draft:
**I Don't Recall** begins with a count of three, as if the band were about to play a happy song. Then the first claim lands: "I can't remember anything at all." It's a strange thing to sing over a tune built to stay in your head. The narrator says the past has been wiped clean, yet every following line is memory: the life they knew, the love they shared, the person who is gone. The amnesia is a defense, and the song shows that it doesn't work.

Look at how the second verse turns. After insisting on forgetting, the narrator admits "And all the love we shared is true." That isn't someone who can't recall. It's someone who recalls too well and would rather not. The verse also makes room for the other person, for "what you lost inside, inside of you," so the grief isn't only the narrator's. Both people lost something, and the song keeps that in view. Then comes the line that sums it up: "But it's hard to go." The life is over, and leaving it is still hard. Nothing gets resolved. The last line sets loss and longing side by side one more time, with the life they shared gone and things still hard without the other person.

The arrangement doesn't add any drama. Arpeggiated acoustic guitar rings clean and bright. Brushes on the snare keep a soft, steady beat that never pushes. The voice is clear and high, held in long, smooth lines, and a second voice joins in harmony. Everything sits in a modest room with natural reverb, polished but not crowded, and the arrangement holds that shape without building. The calm is the trick. A song this gentle about a loss this complete sounds like someone keeping their composure on purpose.

It's the third track on *Incorruptible Heart*, Lavender Diamond's second album, which followed *Imagine Our Love* on Matador in 2007. Becky Stark had piled up a huge number of songs. Her childhood friend Damian Kulash of OK Go, a fellow Brown alum, suggested she treat them as one batch and offered to produce. He also played on the record, and he shares the writing credit here with Stark, Steve Gregoropoulos, Ronald Rege Jr. and Jeff Rosenberg. Dave Fridmann of the Flaming Lips mixed it. The album draws on 1950s pop, disco and electronic sounds, and this song uses the plainest part of that range: brushed drums, close harmony, a melody you could hum after one listen.

The band later made a video with Jena Malone directing, modeled on Andrew Wyeth's *Christina's World*. They described it as a lighthearted, funny look at the therapeutic side of getting over a broken heart. That fits. The song never wallows. It tries to get better and gets caught telling on itself.

It sticks because you hear someone say they've forgotten and then spend three minutes proving they haven't, and the sweet tune makes the lie easy to forgive.
